title: Pythagoras in 3D & Coordinates
welcome_lead: Stretch yourself — Pythagoras in 3D cuboids, distance between coordinate points, and checking if a triangle is right-angled.
meta_desc: GCSE Maths Pythagoras' Theorem stretch — 3D diagonals of cuboids, distance between coordinates, and right-angle verification.
final_note: You can find 3D cuboid diagonals, distances between points and verify right-angled triangles using a² + b² = c².

walkthroughs.body_html:
A cuboid has a space diagonal going from one corner straight through to the opposite corner.

Use Pythagoras twice, or this one-line shortcut:

d = √(a² + b² + c²)

Example: a cuboid measures 2 × 3 × 6.

d² = 2² + 3² + 6² = 4 + 9 + 36 = 49 → d = 7.

(Nice round answer — exams love this.)

To find the straight-line distance between points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), draw a right-angled triangle with horizontal and vertical legs.

d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²)

Example: distance from (1, 2) to (4, 6).

Δx = 4 − 1 = 3, Δy = 6 − 2 = 4.

d² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 → d = 5. (3-4-5 again!)

To test if a triangle has a right angle:

1) Identify the longest side — call it c.
2) Compute a² + b² (the two shorter sides squared and added).
3) If it equals c², the triangle IS right-angled. If not, it isn't.

Example: sides 6, 8, 10. Longest = 10. 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². Yes — right-angled.

Example 2: sides 4, 5, 7. Longest = 7. 4² + 5² = 16 + 25 = 41, but 7² = 49. 41 ≠ 49, so not right-angled.

mcqs.q: Can Pythagoras' theorem be used on any triangle?
options: Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
Yes — it works on any triangle as long as you square the sides.
Sin(2x) equals sin(x)^2 by analogy with squaring.
No — it only applies to right-angled triangles.

mcqs.q: In Pythagoras' theorem, which side does c^2 represent?
options: The hypotenuse — the longest side, opposite the right angle.
Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
c^2 represents the side opposite the largest angle that is not 90 degrees.
c^2 represents any side of the triangle as long as the other two are squared.
No — sin is not a linear function; sin(2x) = 2 sin(x) cos(x).
Only on equilateral triangles because all sides are equal.
Sin(2x) equals sin(x)^2 by analogy with squaring.
Sin is a function, so sin(2x) = 2 sin(x) by pulling the constant out.
